diagnostic_evidence.quote: By convention, the inner product $\Dotp{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Hilb}$ is linear in the first argument.

To prove the equivalent representation, fix $\Tensor{X} = \Matrix{x}^{(1)} \circ \cdots \circ \Matrix{x}^{(d)}$ and let $\Bentry{a}(\Tensor{X}) = \sum_{\mIndex{i}} \Bentry{a}_{\mIndex{i}} x_{\mIndex{i}} \in \Hilb$.

issues.failure_explanation: With the stated convention, the left side equals the inner product of a(conjugate(X)) with h, not that of a(X) with h. For H=C, A=(1,i), X=(1,i)/sqrt(2), and h=1, the asserted equality reads sqrt(2)=0. The final maximized representation is true, but it requires a conjugation change of variables that the proof does not make.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use a(conjugate(X)) in the fixed-X identities and explicitly observe that conjugating all unit vectors leaves the maximization domain unchanged.
issues.overall_effect: The complex-field proof of the equivalent spectral-norm formula, and the subsequent norm-comparison route using it, is defective.
issues.title: Missing complex conjugation in the spectral-norm proof
issues.why_classification: A local conjugation and change-of-variables correction preserves all statements and the full real/complex scope.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: for norms $\Norm{\cdot}{\circ}$ on $\F^{n}$ and $\Norm{\cdot}{\bullet}$ on $\Hilb^{m}$, the $\circ \to \bullet$ operator norm

To get a norm that is not equivalent to $\ell_p(\Hilb)$ norms, let $\Hilb$ be the Sobolev space $\Hilb^1_0(0,1)$, take the $\Ell^2(0,1)$ norm and define $\norm{\Bensor{A}} = \max_{\mIndex{i}} \Norm{\Bentry{a}_{\mIndex{i}}}{\Ell^2(0,1)}$.

issues.failure_explanation: Definition:norms permits an arbitrary target norm. Taking m=n=1, H=H^1_0(0,1), and the target norm to be the L^2 norm makes the defined operator norm exactly the L^2 norm of the single entry. The source itself identifies this as inequivalent to the Hilbert norm; H^1_0 is also incomplete in this weaker norm. The following theorem establishes completeness only for the specified canonical norms, not every norm admitted by the definition.

failure_location.quote: The norms from Definition~\ref{definition:norms} being equivalent, they lead to the same notions of convergence and open (and closed) sets. Moreover, the space $\Hilb^{n_1 \times \cdots \times n_d}$ is complete with respect to them.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict these assertions to the ell_p(H), spectral, and ell_p-to-ell_q(H) norms, or require the arbitrary target norm to be equivalent to ell_2(H).
issues.overall_effect: The prose overstates the topological equivalence and completeness guarantees. The narrower Banach-space theorem is unaffected.
issues.title: Arbitrary operator norms are incorrectly declared equivalent and complete
issues.why_classification: The repair withdraws a genuine arbitrary-target-norm guarantee, but leaves a comparable result for all canonical norms treated in the theorem.

issues.failure_explanation: C maps M into ker(AB), but need not map it into ker(B) perpendicular. For H=R, A=[0], B=[1 0], and C=[1;1], one has M=R and L=span((1,0)), whereas C(1)=(1,1) is not in L. Thus the dimension comparison used to prove Frobenius, and consequently the displayed Sylvester proof, is unsupported.

failure_location.quote: Consider $\Matrix{x} \mapsto \Matrix{Cx}$ as an injective linear operator $\Linop{C} : \mathbb{M} \to \mathbb{L}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace C on M by P C, where P is the orthogonal projection onto ker(B) perpendicular. Since BP=B, this map lands in L and is injective on M, so the existing dimension argument applies.
issues.overall_effect: The Frobenius/Sylvester proof and subsequent uses of its rank-equality route have a support gap; the inequalities themselves admit a local repair.
issues.title: The Frobenius proof maps into the wrong subspace
issues.why_classification: One routine finite-dimensional projection repairs the argument without changing any rank or singular-value claim.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Note that $\Matrix{B}^\pinv \Matrix{B} = \Matrix{I}_{m}$ and $\Matrix{C} \Matrix{C}^\pinv = \Matrix{I}_{n}$, then substitute $\Matrix{C}^\pinv \Batrix{A}^\pinv \Matrix{B}^\pinv$ into Theorem~\ref{theorem:pinv_bochner}.

issues.failure_explanation: The rank hypotheses do not ensure the self-adjoint Penrose equations. Already for H=R, take A=diag(1,0), B=[[1,1],[0,1]], and C=I_2. Then BAC=A and its pseudoinverse is A, whereas C†A†B†=[[1,-1],[0,0]]. The proof's two cancellation identities do not make the resulting projections orthogonal.

failure_location.quote: If $\Matrix{B} \in \F^{k \times m}$ has full column rank and $\Matrix{C} \in \F^{n \times l}$ has full row rank, $(\Matrix{B} \Batrix{A} \Matrix{C})^\pinv = \Matrix{C}^\pinv \Batrix{A}^\pinv \Matrix{B}^\pinv$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the stated rank assumptions by sufficient metric conditions, such as B*B=I and CC*=I. Separately justify the full-column/full-row factorization identity used in the CUR proof.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed covariance of the Moore–Penrose inverse under arbitrary full-rank scalar factors is false. The later CUR argument uses the stricter, valid full-column/full-row product case rather than this general law.
issues.title: False pseudoinverse reverse-order law for full-rank factors
issues.why_classification: A comparable reverse-order statement survives, but only after a substantive restriction of the allowed factors and a contained clarification of the valid product case.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Even when $\Hilb$ is infinite-dimensional, extensions of the most used matrix and tensor norms to the Bochner case are pairwise equivalent.

issues.failure_explanation: A closed nonconvex subset of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space need not contain a nearest point. For example, {(1+1/j)e_j : j>=1} is closed in ell_2 but its distance from zero is not attained. The rank-constrained set needs its own attainment argument; its closedness does not supply one.

failure_location.quote: Since $\mathbb{M}_{\preccurlyeq (\rho,\kappa)}$ is closed, there is a minimizer $\Batrix{C}_\ast \in \mathbb{M}_{\preccurlyeq (\rho,\kappa)}$ of $\Norm{\Batrix{A} - \Batrix{C}}{\ell_2(\Hilb)}$ over $\mathbb{M}_{\preccurlyeq (\rho,\kappa)}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Project every candidate entry onto the finite-dimensional span of stock(A). Show that this preserves both rank upper bounds and cannot increase the error, then obtain a minimizer from a bounded minimizing sequence in that finite-dimensional closed set.
issues.overall_effect: The first HOSVD error estimate remains established, but the existence assertion and the minimum formulation of the quasioptimal comparison are not justified by the supplied proof.
issues.title: Closedness alone does not establish the Tucker minimizer
issues.why_classification: A contained finite-dimensional reduction preserves the theorem and its infinite-dimensional scope, but it is an additional attainment argument, not a consequence of closedness.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: When $n_{\mathrm{rook}} = 0$, the rows are selected at random and the choice of columns is adaptive.

issues.failure_explanation: For the explicitly used setting n_rook=0, the loop never assigns i_*, yet the routine returns it. ABCD then overwrites its previously sampled row index with this undefined output. Thus the pseudocode does not implement the zero-round experiment described in the prose. The usual rook routine has the same omission.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Explicitly allow zero rounds in the outer algorithms and skip the rook call in that case, retaining the already selected row and column. Keep the standalone rook routine restricted to positive rounds, or extend its input to include an initial row.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised zero-round execution of ABCD and hence ABCDX is not defined by the supplied algorithms.
issues.title: Zero-round rook pivoting has no defined row output
issues.why_classification: A local branch or initialization change implements the stated zero-round behavior without changing any approximation or rank guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let us restrict the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ to intervals $[0, \alpha_{\max}]$ and $[0, \beta_{\max}]$, respectively, and approximate two variants of the solution map:
In our experiment, we choose $\alpha_{\max} = \beta_{\max} = 2$, $m = n = 100$, and $K = 75$.

issues.failure_explanation: The stated differential operator acts on sin(kx) by k^2-alpha^2, not k^2+alpha^2. For alpha=1/2, beta=0, its required first coefficient is 8/3, while the displayed formula gives 8/5. The same operator inconsistency hides resonances in the advertised rectangle: at alpha=1, beta=0, testing the equation against sin(x) gives 0=2, so no weak solution exists. Thus the positive-resolvent formula cannot support the claimed solution map over [0,2]^2.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Explicitly reformulate the test problem with the coercive operator -u''+alpha^2 u, which supports the displayed alpha factor throughout the rectangle. If retaining the original operator, use k^2-alpha^2, impose nonresonance, and revise the parameter domain and experiment accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The alpha-dependent solution formula and the full-rectangle solution-map interpretation of the ODE experiment are invalid, independently of the beta-coefficient error.
issues.title: The experiment uses a positive α-resolvent for a negative, resonant operator
issues.why_classification: A comparable two-parameter Dirichlet example survives through a contained reformulation, but the particular operator or parameter-domain promise must change.

issues.failure_explanation: The sine integral of cos(beta x) is k[1-(-1)^k cos(beta pi)]/(k^2-beta^2), with a removable limit at beta=k. The displayed denominator k^2+beta^2 is therefore wrong even when alpha=0, where there is no operator-sign or resonance issue. For alpha=0, beta=1, k=2, the required solution coefficient is 1/3 rather than the stated 1/5. Changing the alpha-dependent operator does not repair this error.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the beta Fourier factor and its removable limits, then recompute the PDE experiment. Alternatively, explicitly identify the existing series test as a synthetic Hilbert-valued family and withdraw its interpretation as the stated BVP solution.
issues.overall_effect: The sampled series is not the claimed cosine-forced solution family, so the reported ODE-specific numerical comparisons are not established for that family.
issues.title: The forcing's sine coefficients have the wrong β denominator
issues.why_classification: The correction changes the sampled data or the mathematical interpretation of the experiment; it is more than a notation fix, but a comparable contained test remains possible.
